I was mobilised on the 20th of September, on the basis of a decision, and in a normal state, one knows which is the authority under the mobilisation of the police force, whether it was the Presidency or somebody, I wouldn't know. What I can say is that the force was, to put it that way, made of people coming from all ethnic groups. That is completely normal, if I may call it that. It was just regular, normal mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you know why were you mobilised on the 20th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: I think that it was because of the events in neighbouring Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you were mobilised, can you tell us if you were issued with anything, that is, with any gear, with any weapons or clothes or what?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes. In the early days, but I mean within a few months or so, we were issued with Kalashnikovs, that is, with long tubes, and we also were given a set of ammunition. And what I can tell about myself is that quite a number of us, but I wouldn't know the exact number, but most of us were, until about -- until about March perhaps we were assigned to guard the building of the television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until March 1992, you tell us, that you were guarding the television building in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes, until about that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: As of March 1992, what was your assignment then? Where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: I was in the police station, except that after the barricades which then happened, I was again, to put it that way, I continued to guard the television. But my shift -- my shift would finish its -- that is, my group would finish its shift and we were then -- because the situation was not normal, we were also asked to come back to the police station. So once the shift would be over, we would go to the police station, and there be on the alert. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you tell us that you were guarding the television building, can you tell us where is the television building in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I told you that I would remind you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's no problem, but the interpreters really cannot follow you if it goes that quick.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. The television building is in Alipasino Polje II, but across the street from so-called Faza A, Phase A.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that after the barricades were put up in March, you were given a different assignment. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Only temporarily, only until the situation calmed down, and then I was again sent to guard the television building, to my usual post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when did you guard the radio/television, as usual? Until when was it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Until about August, or maybe September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be more precise, are you talking about 1992?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel also break after the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us what kind of gear did you have after 1992 and what kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: I had long barrels and ammunition, and uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind both of you. That's what happens now. I know it. It's just we have to enable the interpreters to do their job. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Until August 1992, where was your workplace?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: At the radio/television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether, as a reserve policeman, and although your workplace was at the radio/television, did you also have a police station where you reported and submitted your report whilst you worked?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where was that police station?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: At Alipasino Polje II, but it was about a hundred metres above the television building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer: At this police station where you reported for duty and where you were given your assignments, how many of you were in the police reserve force?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: This is not easy to answer. At the television building there could have been about 30, and all in all, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- and when I say "you," I mean the reserve police force, and specifically, I mean those 30 of you who were guarding the television building -- did you all have your gear and weapons?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, with this gear and this armament, until August 1992, did you go to your police station; that is, would you be carrying these arms and gear on your way to and from the police station?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Now and then, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you tell us that in 1992 -- that until August 1992 you guarded the television building in Sarajevo. Can you tell us: As of August 1992, what was your assignment then in your capacity as a reserve policeman, if you were a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes, I was a reserve policeman. Meanwhile, sometime in June or July, thereabouts -- I'm not sure -- some detachment -- some detached police stations were set up. That is, every phase had its police station, a kind of a subsidiary, and in the one that I was, there were about 30 men all together, and that was the -- it was called the Police Station Phase A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you were at the police station where there were 30 of you at the Phase A.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that Phase A in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: In Alipasino Polje locality, were there any other phases which had their police stations?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically in Alipasino Polje, can you tell us how many phases were there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: A, B, and C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where was the seat of Phase A, that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: On Medjunara [phoen] Square, number whether 9 or 10, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Phases C and B in Alipasino Polje, where did they have their police stations?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Phase C had its police station on Nezavic [phoen] Square, Independence Square, I think, and phase B, I don't know, because I never went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge how many people were there in Phases B and C? You said there were 30 men in Phase A.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Not exactly 30; 30-ish. But considering we had the same duties and assignments and tasks, I think each one had roughly the same number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you, in A phase and the reserve force in B and C, did you also have weapons and equipment?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that about A phase, but I believe the others had the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of weapons you had?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Long-barrel, a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me, I would like to show the witness a part of the map, a portion of the map, that the witness had already indicated when asked by my learned colleagues. My intention is to ask the witness to mark on the map those locations where the police stations were in Alipasino Polje, as far as he can remember. I think we can use the map, the same used by my learned colleagues, perhaps with a different colour. But I do have enough number of copies of that portion of the map, and perhaps there would be other questions as to asking the witness to indicate other locations on the map, if you'll allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic. As far as I can see, the map has been premarked also in blue, so that if we use the black, thick marker, that should not be ... Oh, you have new copies. Okay. That's fine. Yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, what would you prefer? We can use the one already used, so we limit the number of ... But if you say, "I'd rather use the new one," that's fine, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can use that map. I think we'll have a more complete picture and more clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The old map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You even understand that already in B/C/S. That's 3115 we're using now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dziho, could you indicate for us on this map, in the portion which is called Alipasino Polje, could you mark, as far as you can remember, where the police stations were of those phases that you can remember. You can say "A" -- you can put "A," "B," and "C."

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: This is A, C. As for A and for C, I can indicate accurately, but I cannot indicate B. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you give us this answer: In the course of 1992, from August, until September 1994, were you always a member of the reserve force of the C phase of the police station, and what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: From -- until about mid-1994, I was in the reserve police force, after which I went to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic to work on the problems of accommodation, because I'm a social worker, and to work as a social worker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, from August until the end of August 1994, as a member of the police force, were you also engaged in the army?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say "the army," in this period, did you have any task which would take you to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us in which year, or rather, in which period between August 1992 and August 1994 and in which front lines did you go to?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Our task mostly, when we went to the front lines, or rather, to the area of responsibility, as far as the police force members were concerned, was that we would give the troops a rest, and if the front line in that particular location regarding the area of responsibility which was to do with the Novi Grad Police Station, we would go if there was a critical situation, and then we would be sent as reinforcement to the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us in which part of the city were you at the front line?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Well, I don't quite know which part of town that was, but we were on several occasions near Doglude [phoen]. I believe that was the name of the location. We went to Stup, Stupsko Brdo. Mostly in those locations, as far as my police station is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark for us on this map where Stupsko Brdo is on this map and which part of the front line that was.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Here is Stupsko Brdo, but where the line is, I cannot tell you. Considering we were guarding -- we were also guarding important facilities. We had a permanent group that was guarding the pensioners -- retirement home, and the building of Oslobodjenje, who were from the Sarajevo Novi Grad Police Station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark the retirement home and Oslobodjenje building, please. Now, could you please put mark 1 and 2 on the map.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, Your Honour, number 1 the witness marked the retirement home, and number 2, the Oslobodjenje building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you also mark Stupsko Brdo for us on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Well, it says here where Stupsko Brdo is. I couldn't tell you really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if there were front lines in this area.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: In which part do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean Stupsko Brdo and this area where it says Stupsko Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to avoid whatever misunderstanding, I see Stupsko Brdo on two locations, although quite near to each other on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think there's actually three locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three. I missed one, then. Could you please guide me, Mr. Ierace, to the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I imagine, Mr. President, you have in mind the two parallel roads marked Stupsko Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I had, as a matter of fact, I see there are now two parallel roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see -- I see that immediately under the home for the elderly people, there are two times parallel Stupsko Brdo, and then, at a rectangular going to the south-west, another what looks as if it is a street also is indicated by Stupsko Brdo. We see a lot of Stupsko Brdos on the map, so, Ms. Pilipovic, could you please -- if you are talking about the area of Stupsko Brdo, if you mean that it would cover the whole area in which we find these names, would you then repeat your question to the witness and let's make sure that there are no misunderstandings. I think your question was about the front lines in that area. Mr. Dziho, have you seen that there are three times Stupsko Brdo on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic was asking you whether you knew where the front lines were situated in that area, and that area by now means the whole area where we find these three indications of Stupsko Brdo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, either I can't see it or you can't see it. There is a little stream -- a river called Dobrinja, and we were then -- we know it because of Stanica Kuce locality. That's how we know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, so we can be more precise, could you tell us in relation to the buildings of the retirement home and the Oslobodjenje building, could you perhaps tell us in relation to these buildings and the Stupsko Brdo, could you tell us where the front lines were?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Well, it was probably something like this, in relation to this area, up to this intersection here, but I don't know any further really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to the Institute for the Blind of the locality, do you know where the front line was?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No. No. But it was more further towards this direction, because the Serbian forces covered this part of the area. I don't know how much you know. But also the then market, and it's a market now, they had it under their control. And I believe there's also a barracks there. So it was quite a large area of Stupsko Brdo which was under the control of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please circle it, according to your recollection.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the Oslobodjenje building and the Ante Babica Street, in this area, where was the front line?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Do you mean here, in between -- between the Institute for the Blind and the Oslobodjenje building? There was like a field there, like a meadow, and this was, if we can call it that, no-man's-land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, since you were guarding the Oslobodjenje building and the retirement home, were there soldiers, and which unit was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No, there were no soldiers. This was under our control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: In relation to the building, to the part of the Alipasino Polje and Ante Babica Street, was there a front line there, and could you mark it for us, please.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No, the front line was not there. As far as I can recall, the front line was the Institute for Blind Children, and then further deeper into the Nedzarici locality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the Institute for Blind Children and part of the locality where it says "Street of Djure" Street, could you mark there where the front line was?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: As far as Djure Street is concerned, this is within the Vojnicko Polje area, and since there was no need, I never went there, so I wouldn't know where the line was. But in general, I know that practically there, if we're talking about classical trenches, there were no trenches there, no typical trenches, because people defended from those first front houses that were probably destroyed. But I don't know, because I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say "probably destroyed" and you didn't go there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Well, it was the usual practice of the Serb army. Whatever they did was to first level everything out with shells and grenades and cannons, so nobody could live there in front. And if it was not destroyed, then they would set fire to it with incendiary bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did You go to see such incidents?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: In Dobrinja V. Then you also have the same situation in Ante Babica Street, where the entire facade of the house is pock-marked with shell pieces and grenades of all calibres, and they fired at apartment blocks where people lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you were so well informed about that area, perhaps you have information about the building of the Institute for Blind Children and the buildings in that area that you say were under the Bosnian Serb army control. What kind of situation were these buildings in? Did you have opportunities to see that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us specifically about the buildings surrounding the Institute for the Blind and these buildings around? What was their state?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Most of the buildings, particularly nearer to Mojmilo, it was all destroyed. It was shelled, but it was shelled by the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that it was shelled by the Serb army, can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Perhaps from the beginning, practically. First there was much sniping, and as time went on, from mid-1992 onwards, there was heavy artillery fire on all parts of the city, particularly on the edge parts, rim parts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark on the map these edge parts of the city that you say that were shelled by the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No, I can't find my bearings on this map. But what it says here, Ante Babica Street, we called it the Tenth Transversal, and Ante Babica was called this entire block of buildings which was near to this parking -- next to this parking place. And this street here, this street here, which went out onto the Brigada [phoen] Street, the main street, we called that the Tenth Transversal. This area here, rather, this health centre, medical centre, it was completely destroyed. The Serb army shelled it. And here, in this part, all these buildings that were here, these houses here along the Tenth Transversal, all this was completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you are explaining this to us, do you have any knowledge whether you know on the other side, on the other side of the transversal, near the Mojmilo Brdo, what army controlled that side?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Do you mean Mojmilo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: At the very beginning, in 1992, I think June or July, on the top of the Mojmilo hill, there was a unit of -- a JNA unit, which I believe had one or two tanks, or a couple of tanks, and they also had two armoured vehicles, and they fired on the Mojmilo locality, where people lived. And they also fired on the C phase, since they could see the C phase. When they withdrew, I believe it was in July and August, I think. Then they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we talking July, August 1992?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about 1992. After that, that was under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to return to the Institute for the Blind. Could you tell us whether in 1994 or 1995 you were able to see the Institute for the Blind and the buildings surrounding it, and could you describe for us what state these buildings were in?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: At that time there was no need for me to go there. Since I did not go there -- because I work on completely different part of town, so there was no need for me to go there, or any purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you never went to this part of town?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: After I moved to the republic MUP, no, I didn't go, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us: When was the first time that you went to that part of town and saw the Institute for the Blind, if you ever saw it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes. After the ceasefire, after the reintegration, I then -- after the trams started working again, I then went and passed through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what the building looked like?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: It looked the same as it looked in 1993. I think approximately, because the Institute for Blind Children -- there were several places from which the sniper fired. I remember that. There were locations for snipers. I remember that. The rest, I didn't really pay much attention to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be absolutely precise, did you see that in 1993 or did you see that after the Dayton was signed, the Institute for the Blind, the state that you're describing it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: In 1993 and after the Dayton was signed. If you're asking me was it destroyed, as far as I could see, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the buildings surrounding the Institute for the for the Blind? Were they destroyed?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No. As far as I could see from a safe distance, no, not significantly, if I can say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "safe distance," what is that safe distance?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: The further, the better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you, Witness, what distance that was that you saw these buildings from.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: From the Oslobodjenje building and from the retired people's home building, and partially from the Centre for Blind Children, you can see it. You can also see it from the parking place, where we happened to be at the time, my colleague and I, when we were at the place of the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you went to help the army as a reinforcement, could you tell us what kind of help was it that you gave?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: This was help in terms of manpower, depending on the situation in the field. If there was a danger to the line, that the front line would fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us to which unit were you sent as reinforcement, as help? What was the unit that was there to the area that you were sent to?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: I don't know. It was BH army. Which unit, I really couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what were the members of that unit -- what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: All kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: To start with, they were dressed, if they didn't have anything similar to camouflage uniform, they were wearing civilian clothes. I mean, they were wearing civilian clothes because there was no equipment, there were no weapons, so that's how people went to the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say there was no equipment, there were no weapons, are you saying there were no weapons whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes, there were weapons, but these weapons were procured, if I can say it, when members of Serb nationality left, then in their apartments, all kinds of weapons were found in their apartments: Long-barreled guns, grenades, machine-guns, rifles. I remember in 1992, in the locality, it was at Mladzin [phoen], called Mladz [phoen], in the yard, where there was -- in the vegetable garden. There was lettuce and there were onions. They also found some mortar shells. They found some landmines, machine-guns. All kinds of weaponry were found there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you found this, were you part of a team which found all this?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're telling us all this according to what you've heard?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: According to what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you if you were there. Did you see the weapons?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: I saw the weapons. I didn't go personally to search these apartments, but as someone who was patrolling and was patrolling a locality, I was in a position to see when people who did it, they were then taking these weapons out, three or four rifles, snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what people were there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were present when the BH army was taking the weapons from these houses, can you tell us who lived in these houses?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: The Serbs who left. I don't know when. Who departed, who left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they left?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: They probably chose their side, although I have to say that in my unit and in other units, as far as I know, I had colleagues of Serb ethnicity, of Croat ethnicity. We were a station -- I'm talking about my station -- and later on as well, they were members of the police force as well as of the army, the BH army. They were all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where were these weapons with the BH army placed?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it was distributed -- all these weapons were distributed among the combatants who had no weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now you tell us that the BH army used machine-guns and rifles and grenades?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, since in 1992 and 1993 and 1994, as a member of the reserve police force in Phase A, and you say that you guarded the building of Oslobodjenje and the retired people's home, was there any fighting in those areas where you were? Were there any -- was there any armed conflict between the parties of the conflict in those areas?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Not when I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say when you were there --

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: When I was on duty, when there were no operations at all except that -- and I don't know exactly when. In 1992, when the Serb forces destroyed the big Oslobodjenje building, following that, as far as I know, the police came to guard the Oslobodjenje, and it was there throughout -- because Oslobodjenje came out throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you tell us that there were no armed conflicts when you were on duty. Did you hear from other colleagues of yours? Did they take part in any armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No. This side, insofar as the retired people's home is concerned, or the Oslobodjenje building, since in front of them there was a meadow, if I can call it that, a lawn, it was quite quiet there apart from some sniper fire. I'm referring to the period when we took over the guarding of those two buildings. I don't know what went on there before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I didn't want to interrupt you when you used the same time because I felt that it was a subject which had -- of quite some importance for you, but now we are five minutes over that time. Could you please indicate how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try to be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us a moment ago that there was some sniper action. Can you tell us if, in the police reserve force and in the BH army, there were any snipers?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No, not in the police force, as far as I know; and as for the army, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I have to note that you are refusing to tell the truth. I now have a couple of questions regarding the photograph 3279Oa. It is 9755/3. That was the only photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there seems to be one of the rare occasions, perhaps the first occasion, that my learned colleague appears to be complying with Rule 90. I'd be grateful if she could be a little bit more specific as to which part of this witness's evidence is inconsistent with the Defence case. I'm referring, of course, to page 62, line 11 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please indicate, Ms. Pilipovic, where you said that you had to note that the witness was refusing, in your view, to tell the truth. What exactly --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness is refusing to tell the truth when I asked him if in the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were any snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I see the answer of the witness: No, not in the police force, as far as I know; and as for the army, I do not know. The mere fact that if you could establish that there were snipers in the police forces, the answer of the witness does not for sure say that there were not in the police forces as far as I know. But please proceed and we'll see what your next question will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I can put a question to the witness so that you can make your ruling about the snipers in the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the witness have any knowledge whether in the BH police, that is, the republican police, were those special sniper units called [indiscernible] Police? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't call it that. That was not a special sniper unit. That was a special unit of the Ministry of the Interior set up for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a session purpose in peacetime. In peacetime, everybody was together until the majority of members of Serb origin walked out. So it was a peacetime special unit for special purposes, an anti-terrorist unit, if I may call it that. That's what they're called nowadays. So it wasn't a special sniper unit, especially not a special sniper unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that this unit did not operate as a special sniper unit during the armed conflict in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No, it did not as a special sniper unit. No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you have before you the photograph which you mark to show where the barricades were and where, to your recollection, was the Home of the Blind people. Can you also mark on this photograph the place where you were, if, of course, it is shown in this photograph. If not, will you please draw a line to show where you and your colleague were at the time when you saw the first man.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: This would be the extension of this photograph. Now I know that this is east here. And you see here, right next to the edge of the picture, you can see this grass patch, this grassy belt. And it stretches as far as the parking lot, which is over here. Now, there is about a metre and a half to three metre altitude difference, depending on where you go. That is, there is a slope here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you then show the pedestrian crossing here, and can you mark, if you were near this pedestrian crossing, or is it that we cannot see the area where you were?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: You mean this pedestrian crossing or this one here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This one here. This one here. I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from the speed, I think I can hear that the interpreters have to go on a higher speed, higher and higher, so there will be a point where I have to remind you again to pause now and then. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned colleague during the cross-examination has repeatedly invited the witness to refer to various locations on the map and now on the photograph without then recording orally the areas indicated by the witness, which will make it extremely difficult to make any sense of this transcript when we return to it at a later stage of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if perhaps my friend could indicate for the record, for instance, to give an example, which of the five pedestrian crossings that appear in the photograph the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, I was approximately at the point to ask the same. Let me just give you the first start. When the witness talked about the grassy patch, he was indicating with the pointer the lowest part -- lowest horizontal part of the picture, which, as we know from his earlier evidence, would be the eastern part of the Ante Babica. And perhaps you could indicate where the witness pointed at when he was talking about the pedestrian crossings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you just now, when you pointed at the east part of the street, did you point at a zebra which is at the bottom of the photograph? Is that the pedestrian crossings in the vicinity of which you were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Ms. Pilipovic, that we get some misunderstandings now. If this would assist you, please repeat the question, and I'll, for the sake of the record, indicate exactly where the witness points at. Because if you're now talking about east, I'm afraid, as a matter of fact, that you're referring to the south. Because what is left on the picture is not to the left on the map. What is left on the picture is at this moment on the south of the map. So if you -- please proceed, give me one or two seconds now and then to assist you, and if I'm wrong, please indicate so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you indicate the place on this photograph where you and your colleague were at the time when you saw the first injured, the injured number 1.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: When we heard the shots, you cannot see it. We were in the parking lot, so that we could not see. We had neither the visual or any other contact with the injured person, because the parking lot is on a high ground, that is, two or three metres above this pedestrian lane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark in this photograph the place where you saw the injured number 1, if I may call him that.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: About here, roughly, where you can see these trees or this bush.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you place an "X" there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Fine, so that I don't have to describe it. The witness was first indicating when he said the parking lot, he was indicating at the very lower part of the picture, which -- and he made clear that the parking lot, as such, was below it, and not on the picture. Would you please mark the place where you saw the victim with an "X," Mr. Dziho, and please do it with a black marker. The black marker is there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: About here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put number 1 there.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark on this photograph, or can one see the place where the person number 2 was?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No, you can't see it here. He was in this area over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us near the parking lot? Because I know that there is a parking lot behind there.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: The parking lot is here, roughly, and then you have this green belt here. You see this roof. This is a structure, this is a building which was built after the war. And the parking lot is about here. And the injured person was over here, you cannot see it. It was more to the right and eastward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the witness is pointing at the right bottom corner, especially where there is a pedestrian crossing, which goes on the picture from left to right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The witness can draw an arrow, and that can serve as a sign for what you have just said for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness now has marked with a small cross a place just outside of the photograph, in one of the margins. Is that where the parking lot is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And a bit further on, more further on, even more further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More down, more to the right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any knowledge, since you told us that you were in contact with the Franjic family, did you receive information about which one of these witnesses was injured first, as the counsel says?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the incident happened, did you learn which one of the witnesses, number 1 or number 2, fell the first?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Ivan Franjic was the first one, and I think he was the first one, and we went to his wife. I think it was his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know: At the time when Ivan Franjic -- when Witness Ivan Franjic fell, did you know where was Witness 2 in relation to him?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: You mean the injured number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't know whether there's any translation problem or that you're using your own language a bit confusing. Again, when the persons are -- the person you're referring to are in the English translation referred to as "witnesses," where I would expect you to use the word "victims," since I especially -- a deceased person can hardly be expected to be a witness. I don't know whether it's your language or the translation, but ... Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have before me the statement of the witness Franjic, and that is what got me confused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us: Victim number 2, in relation to Victim number 1, in what -- what was his position when Victim 1 fell? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when in contact with the family and Victim 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to slow down, and it's very difficult also for you, Mr. Dziho, because you have no moving text any more on your screen, so you don't know when to pause. But we really have to slow down. And perhaps if I may suggest to you, Ms. Pilipovic, that Victim 1 and Victim 2 is perhaps always not as clear as well, so perhaps if you just use the names of those that have been described as victims. That means Ivan Franjic or Augustin Vucic, that perhaps that would be helpful for you to talk about the victim that had been wounded and the victim that had, in the testimony of this witness, had been killed. Perhaps that makes it more clear to whom you are referring. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us: From the place where you were -- in relation to -- that is, and looking towards the students' hostel can you tell us if from that place where one can see the Home of the Blind in relation to the students' hostel

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: I really don't understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained to us the spot you were standing at the time when you saw that Victim Ivan Franjic and late Augustin Vucic were in positions as you explained. Now, looking from the spot where you were in relation to the students' hostel, can one from that place see the Home for the Blind?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: I don't know which point in time you have in mind exactly. You mean whether we heard the shots or when we started running towards Ivan Franjic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the moment when the shots were heard.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: We were standing in the parking lot and we could see that, we could see the Home for the Blind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Ierace -- Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, the Defence also objects to this part of the witness's statement. The Defence went out to the site, and from the position about which the witness said that he was standing there, one cannot see the Home for the Blind from this position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the point, Ms. Pilipovic, and as you know, commenting is not at this moment what you are expected to do. Mr. Ierace, has the Prosecution -- does the Prosecution want to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Re-examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you have the photograph in front of you, I direct your attention to the cross that you placed in the bottom right-hand corner of the margin. Does that cross indicate where you found Mr. Vucic or does it indicate where the car park was, and therefore, where you were when you heard the shots?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: This is where we found Mr. Augustin, a little bit further on, and we were about here, that is, in the parking lot, and you cannot see it on this photograph, to the east, so that we had the visual contact with the Home for the Blind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you please place a 2 alongside the cross where you found the person you referred to as Augustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please now use the -- would you please now use the blue marker again. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand your evidence to be that, in fact, the victim was further down the photograph and further to the right of the photograph than the margin allows. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please now go to the other cross, that is, the cross which appears in the bottom left-hand corner of the photograph. I understand your evidence to be that that is the approximate position in which you found Mr. Franjic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please place a 1 alongside that cross.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your evidence you referred to a building on that eastern side of Ante Babica, which did not exist at the time of the shooting. You said you could see part of its roof. Would you please circle the part of the roof that you can see.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the building to which you referred?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, will you please indicate with an arrow the direction in which the car park was in which you were standing when you heard the two shots. And that arrow could come from the closest part of what appears in the photograph to the car park, to that spot in the car park.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, Mr. Dziho? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Ierace asked you to make an arrow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to make an arrow from the place closest to where you were on the parking lot, so an arrow from a place -- which appears on the photograph. So find the place on the photograph which is nearest to where you were at the parking spot -- parking lot and then make an arrow in the direction of where you actually were. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, during cross-examination you were shown the map and you referred to various places on the map, including along Ante Babica, which you said received heavy fire from the Bosnian Serb army side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not a proper -- it's not one building; it is a skyscraper, a 15-storey high, and you have a number of entrances. That is, it is a large residential block, apartment block.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, assuming that the photograph in front of you was taken from a building, would the building from which the photograph was taken be consistent with one of the buildings that you described as receiving heavy fire from the Bosnian Serb army side?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you went to the area of Institute for the Blind after the ceasefire. That is, I took you to mean after the cessation of hostilities in 1995 between the opposing parties in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: It could have been even later, 1996 or maybe 1997, and I rode past it in a car, because down this street there is a company -- there is a florist. There is a company, horticultural company, people who grow flowers and sell flowers, and with my family I went there to buy some flowers. Possibly I did not pass there before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to that visit, you said there were several places from which the sniper fired. I remembered that. There were locations for snipers. What did you actually see that caused you to say those words?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Well, in a manner of speaking, two buildings dominated Nedzarici: The Institute for Blind Children, and the Faculty for Theology. It was the tallest building in that area and it was common knowledge that it was one of the snipers strongholds. So the Faculty of Theology and the Institute for Blind Children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you drove past, did you notice anything about the buildings that made up the Institute for the Blind that indicated they were used by snipers?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Well, they had, as I already said it, they had those rifle openings through which they opened fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain in more detail what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: These are openings in walls, not natural openings. I mean, they are not windows or doors, but in a wall, you break through at one or two levels. Openings were made, some 30, 40 centimetres wide perhaps, through which the snipers fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt you right at the moment where I felt it might be a point of importance to you as well. On the other hand, we are close to 6.00 already, so if you say it's just one question, then I'll ask for some leniency from the interpreters' booth. But if it's more, we should have a break now, if at least this is a moment that -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It may be more than one, so I think it's better to have a break now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll -- let me just see. Then we'll adjourn until five minutes past 6.00. It's relatively short, but it took a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, you were re-examining the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that the name of the street that runs from the School for the Blind to the intersection which appears on the left of the photograph in front of you, which is P3279 Oa, is called Branka Bujica Street. When you observed the sniper holes in the walls of the Institute for the Blind buildings, did you notice any such holes on the sides of those buildings which face towards the intersection of Branka Bujica Street and Ante Babica?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Well, I would like to say that I did not see bullet holes on the Institute for the Blind Children, but I saw openings, holes, for rifles which they used to fire at civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's, in fact, what I was meaning to ask you, whether you noticed any of those holes for sniper fire on the sides of the buildings facing that intersection.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Any of the colleagues, any questions? Judge El Mahdi has a question for you, or perhaps even more. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Witness, you spoke about a ceasefire which was valid at the time of the incident, and you were asked about the behaviour of the citizens and how it changed, or how it changed when there was a ceasefire, in relation to when there was firing and return of fire. So who decided on these ceasefires, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: I don't know who signed. Presumably these ceasefires were signed by the people who were in command, so to speak, in command of the armies, who had the authority, whether it would be a president or somebody from the military structure, I'm not sure. But we're talking about a ceasefire where the people behaved differently. Yes, mostly. But this was a false sense of security, because, as I said earlier, very often it happened during several ceasefires -- I don't know how many there were in all -- that it was during the ceasefire that there were sudden shelling and there was sniping and that this firing caused deaths of civilians. So as to what I said before, we had our duty. Our obligation was to warn the people who perhaps relaxed too much or were too exposed, particularly women and children, because most of the time, depending on the situation in the city itself, whether there was shelling or whether there was stronger sniping, they mostly spent their time in cellars. They didn't have the right conditions, not to say anything about that there was no electricity, no food, water. And people tried to somehow manage, and they were forced to expose themselves. And as the war went on, there was no fuel, there was no wood, firewood, so they had to go to these places that were truly exposed in order to gather some firewood, some -- so they could cook what they had. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, there were several ceasefires, and what you're saying is that the rule was really that it was a non-ceasefire rather than a ceasefire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And what was the rhythm of that non-ceasefire? Was it the first time? Was it customary for the parties -- who was in fact responsible, according to you, for the breaking, violating the ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was the Serb army that was responsible. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So when we're talking about the Institute for the Blind, you said that there were openings that were made with a purpose to use as firing positions; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So the rhythm at which these firings were done, was this continual or was it daily, or were there intervals, or were there long intervals when police had to intervene?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Well, how can I say it? There was no rule really, because we would have a shift, a shift on the front lines. So the shift would be for ten days and then someone else would go for a change of shift. So jokingly, we used to say that a shift arrived, a second shift arrived. Perhaps paramilitary formations would arrive from Serbia or maybe Arkan's men or White Eagles units that we called koker [phoen] shakers, meaning chicken chasers. And mostly when these troops came, they really -- I can say that -- they were absolutely merciless. Whoever put their nose out into the open, they fired. And there was much more intense firing then, in all directions. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] That is, the other party had an easy access to leave and then go to -- and then return to the Centre for the Blind, the Institute for the Blind?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia also has one more question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like you to have a look on the photograph. You have the photograph there? That one. Okay. If we look at the Institute for the Blind Children and to the place of the first victim, where the first victim was found, we see an open space. My question is: Was there that open space at that time, as it is today?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes, except that there were no trees. These trees were not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we have a look to the second place of the second victim, we know that there was the building which we are seeing now, but at that time I think that it was not finished. But except for that, was there at that time an open space as well?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Do you mean in relation to the second wounded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The second wounded, yes.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes. These buildings -- in fact, that's not a building. This was like a kiosk, like a small stand, kiosk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: It was, except for that it was an open space, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dziho, I also have a question for you. You have answered some questions from the Defence about what in the questions was called a special sniper unit, where you said no, this was not a special sniper unit. You explained that this was a unit for special purposes, created already in peacetime, and that it served as an anti-terrorist unit. Could you tell us what you know about the operations of this unit during the conflict? Unfortunately, I cannot recall the name given to it by Ms. Pilipovic, since it was not immediately picked up by the short-hand writers, but you know what unit I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes. This is Vikic's unit. He was a special -- member of special forces even before the war, and during the first few days, when the aggression started, and in relation to the conflict in the city itself. You probably have at your disposal the recordings of the film of when the people gathered in front of the Executive Council, in front of the building of the Executive Council at Marin Dvor, and from the direction of Vrbanja bridge, above Vrbanja bridge, fire was opened on the civilians, and this is where the first civilian victim died. And this bridge is today called the Bridge of Suada Dilberovic, who was a girl killed. She was a student. I don't know how old she was. About 20 something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dziho, I'm sorry for interrupting you. I'm not especially interested in the first stages of the conflict, but do you know anything about this unit in the later stages, summer 1992? Could you tell us anything about the operations of that unit? That's the first question: Under whose command was this unit?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: As far as I know, I don't know until which year. Probably until the end of the war. But the commander was Dragan Vikic. That's why it was called Vikic's unit. And he was very well renowned in the city of Sarajevo. The unit was mostly active, as far as I know, for defensive purposes, and particularly in the beginning of the war, there were certain attacks by tanks and armoured vehicles on the Presidency, and then Vikic's units used anti-tank weapons to defend -- to destroy these few tanks and to defend the Presidency. And this was their purpose mainly. If there was an attack by what we called armoured units, they then would stop the attack of these armoured units. That's as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they on special assignments or were they involved in the conflict at various places? Could you tell us a bit more about it? And perhaps especially also because I think that was part of the questions put to you whether they would use sniper rifles as well as one of their methods or techniques, whatever you would call it.

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know anything more about their involvement in the conflict? You said -- you said they were especially, in the beginning of the war, if there were attacks by tanks and armoured vehicles on the Presidency, that they would then defend the Presidency. But in later stages of the -- because do I understand you well that this is also referring to the early stages of the conflict or ...?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: In order to make it clear, perhaps that's why I'm trying to -- I'm being a little more extensive. But as far as I know, this special unit was based somewhere in the city, where they were on duty, where they were on alert. And after they received a call or an information that there was a shift in the front line, or if there was an armoured unit attack in these -- somewhere, or perhaps an attack with an armoured vehicle, then they would go to the location where there was this combat situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that they were especially called for combat situations. Would that mean that they would not be called on more or less stable front lines or ...?

utterances.speaker: FUAD DZIHO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mr. Dziho, you've had to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. answer a lot of questions, both from the parties, from the Judges. You'll understand that it's very important for the Court to fulfil its task, and it's our tasks to take decisions on the cases that are in front of us. It's very important that all the parties can put questions to the witnesses that have been present during that period, in that area, that we'll get answers to these questions, not only the parties, also the Judges. I thank you very much for coming to The Hague and assisting the Court in what this Court will have to do, and to say take decisions. I know it's a very long way from Sarajevo, so I -- that's perhaps a special reason to thank you, and apart from that, I wish you a safe trip home again. Mr. Usher, would you then please lead Mr. Dziho out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please assist us in going through the documents that have been tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P3279Oa, the photograph marked by the witness; P3115, the map marked by the witness; the death certificate, P2664 in B/C/S and the English translation, P2664.1; the record from the University Medical Centre Sarajevo, P2477, and the English translation, P2477.1; and the report from the public security station, P2476, and the English translation, P2476.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in relation to the 2477 document, which is the document relating to the wounds of Ivan Franjic, the Defence objects to this document because it is illegible and because we do not have the corresponding stamp of the medical centre. And as far as the death certificate is concerned, considering that Mr. Augustin Vucic died, we cannot say that he died -- he died on the 1st of June, 1994. We cannot say that it is related to the incident when he was shot in March 1994, and really, in order to have this exhibit complete, we would have to have a post-mortem report as well as a -- a post-mortem report which would show whether the cause of death was because of the wounding incident, and these are the objections of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, as far as the death certificate, that's number 2644, is concerned, we have ruled in earlier stages of this procedure -- of this proceedings that it's not necessarily from the death certificate that the cause of death is established. This, of course, could have some implications as far as the probative value of the document is concerned. If there's no cause of death, it might be, as such, not good enough to establish any cause of death. I think it's mainly tendered in order to establish that the person mentioned in this document died. Then the second, the illegibility of the medical report, the Chamber does agree with you that parts are not very legible, but that does not mean that this document could have no probative value at all, since other parts are quite legible, even if that would not cover all the words on it. And of course, we'll have to keep in mind that if a document is not very legible, that this might the have some implications as far as the probative value is concerned, and we'll decide on that, of course, at a later stage. But it's not inadmissible as evidence at this very moment. The same is valid as far as the absence of any stamp is concerned, since it is not an absolute requirement for a document to be admitted into evidence that there's a stamp on it, even if you would expect a stamp on such kind of documents. So all the documents tendered are admitted into evidence and all my remarks I made about the probative value might be -- might have been well understood by the Prosecution. I think then, Mr. Ierace, we've still got enough time to call your next witness, and that would be ...? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's Mr. Pita, Mr. President, and that witness will be taken by Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, would you please lead the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pita, as far as I'm informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pita, before giving your testimony -- before giving your testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration will be given to you now by the usher, and I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pita. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you had to wait for a long time. I can already indicate to you that we'll finish at 7.00. That's in 25 minutes. So presumably your examination will be continued tomorrow, but you'll now be first examined by counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Mundis. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President Examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Pita, would you please state your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: Ekrem Pita; the 24th of November, 1949.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pita, you first moved to the city of Sarajevo in 1963; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you lived in the city of Sarajevo constantly from 1963 through to the present?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and always at the same address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The specific address is not necessary, sir, but could you please tell the Trial Chamber what neighbourhood or region of the city you have resided in since 1963.

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: I lived in municipality of Stari Grad, old town, and the neighbourhood area was known as Sirokaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pita, can you tell the Trial Chamber what type of house or what type of dwelling you live in?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: I lived in my own house. It's my house, my own house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do any other families live in your house?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall when the war started in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: The war in Sarajevo started on the 6th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber how your life changed as a result of the war's beginning in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: To put it in a nutshell, it changed 360 degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you elaborate, Mr. Pita?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: Sure. Before the war, I lived very well. We were very well off. No problems or anything. And in all went down the drain when the war started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what type of employment were you engaged when the war started?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: I had a job. I was an electrician and I worked for a large company, Energoinvest, and before the war I had a seniority of 25 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly after the war started in Sarajevo, did you become aware of sniping incidents in the city?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: Well, I learned something here and there around that something happened, that day when the war started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the months after the war started, that would be in the latter half of 1992, did you become aware of sniper activities in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: Yes, and it happened in my neighbourhood too, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the residents of your neighbourhood take any protective measures to avoid being hit by sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: Yes, of course we did, even at home, because my house has a lower part made of concrete, and we spent 90 per cent of our time in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how far was your house from the front lines, or the confrontation lines, during the latter half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: As the crow flies, about 300, 350 metres. I'm really not an expert, so I'm giving you just my own figure, an estimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pita, what were the two forces that were vying for control of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know what forces. I know they were the aggressor forces and there was the defence, that is, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was defending the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The force that you referred to as the aggressor force, was that the Bosnian Serb army, otherwise known by the acronym VRS?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so. It was they and the Yugoslav People's Army, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly after the war began, did you lose electrical power to your house?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: My neighbourhood, the power was cut off. I had no telephone, nor water, or power, as of the 2nd of May. The whole infrastructure went out in my neighbourhood, and my house, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where your family went to obtain water for your household?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: Well, we were trying to manage in different ways to get some household water I went with my girl. But that happened. That was then. It was about 150 metres from my house. And it's not drinking water. Its source is a surface source, and we used that. And then the drinking water, we went to different places where we were allowed to go and take it for our personal consumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The water that you've described as household water, where did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: This is surface water. It was wintertime and we had made it ourselves, my neighbours and I. And in spring and summer, when there would be some water, then we would use it for those purposes. Otherwise, I mean, when there was no water, then there was no water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This surface water, was it draining off of the hill or mountain nearby to where you resided?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: EKREM PITA
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
